prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms held at the magic wavelength are interrogated in large numbers, bringing timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B036 to B012. The reason is scientific, not the count of supporters. In round 1 I wrote that B012 has the cleanest attribution and the most mature confirmation on the shortlist, and that if the committee wants settled understanding it is the safer choice. After reading the full exchange I think the committee should want that. The magic-wavelength lattice is a quantitative idea whose every systematic (lattice light shifts, collisions, blackbody radiation) has been tracked down, and agreement at the 1e-18 level between independent clocks, reproduced in several laboratories and compared over fibre links, is the kind of verified result I keep asking for in this room. The millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and the many-body effects in a lattice of thousands of atoms are results about nature that already exist, so this is not only a tool. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the early demonstrations, and Ye's group brought accuracy and stability to the present level, so the two-name credit follows a clear division. Suggested wording for the citation is narrow: it names the lattice architecture of neutral atoms at the magic wavelength with many-atom interrogation, so it does not read as a general metrology prize or as a repeat of the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: My own earlier lead, B036, is still the more surprising physics: theory predicted flat bands, experiment found correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle, and many laboratories have reproduced the phenomena. The B012 case is weaker on that axis, because it is a measurement method whose fundamental payoffs (varying constants, dark matter searches, geodesy, the redefinition of the second) are still prospective, and it sits next to two recent metrology prizes. There is also real doubt about whether Katori and Ye alone represent the priority record, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and the ion-clock groups did decisive work and I cannot settle early dates from memory. These are reasons for careful wording, not reasons to give B012 up. For B036, the pairing mechanism is open, the experimental credit (Cao, Fatemi, Dean, Young) is not settled, and the Bistritzer share cannot be fixed with the certainty I would want. I would be uncomfortable naming three people on that basis this year.

responses.point: Kroll supports B012 but would prefer a prize about nature rather than a measurement tool, and discloses lineage through John Hall's laboratory, from which Ye also came, while suggesting the 1e-18 accuracy and redshift be tied to Ye and the proposal and early demonstrations to Katori.
responses.response: I think the tool-versus-discovery distinction is real but is answered by the results themselves: two independent clocks agreeing at 1e-18 and resolving a redshift across a millimetre are measured facts about nature, obtained with this architecture. I agree with dividing the credit in the citation as you and Olsson suggest, and my suggested wording above follows it loosely. Your lineage disclosure is the proper kind of record to put in the minutes. It is a distant link with no joint work or financial interest, and I would not treat it as requiring recusal, though that is a matter for the chair and the committee to decide.

responses.point: Mehlig keeps B012 first and B036 and B057 as alternatives, wants the citation worded narrowly around the lattice architecture, and notes that the 2005 and 2012 prizes make a sceptic call this incremental metrology.
responses.response: I accept your wording point and have used it. I do not think the earlier prizes remove the novelty, because the comb gives the clockwork to count optical cycles and ion control gives single-ion clocks, while the neutral-atom magic-wavelength lattice is a different physical regime: many atoms, no Doppler or recoil shift, and the many-body effects that matter. On B036 you described the pairing mechanism as unsettled, and I have to concede the point. I argued that the prize need not rest on it, but my own attribution doubts (Cao, Dean, Bistritzer) point the same way as yours, and I now think the committee would not be able to defend B036 this year as well as it could B012.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B012 but wants a narrow citation, says the redefinition of the second is not a prize criterion, and cannot settle the priority of early strontium demonstrations from memory.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition of the second should not decide timing. A standards-body decision measures a different thing from a physical discovery, and the committee should judge the demonstrated science. On priority, I share your uncertainty and think it is the one real open item for B012. The record from about 2001 to 2005 should be checked before the final ballot, particularly Katori's proposal against Lemonde and the Takamoto and JILA demonstrations. If that check showed that a third name was needed, I would still not support a larger configuration without a strong reason, because the three-person limit is a limit of the credited achievement and not just a number to fill.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B012 because the experiment is clean and every physical detail has been understood, while placing circuit QED (B051) and B010 as alternatives and expressing recusal caution on B051.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of B012, and as a theorist working with materials codes I value exactly the point you make: every detail of the systematics has been tracked down. On your B051 recusal caution, I think it is proper to disclose that field as your own and to keep from leading on it. I do not see B051 as a competitor this year, since superconducting circuits were recognised in 2025 and I want to avoid a prize that looks like a continuation, though I would not want to oppose it by a wide margin in a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson alone prefers IceCube (B029) but accepts that the astrophysical interpretation is incomplete, that three names under-represent a collaboration of hundreds, and that he would not block B012.
responses.response: I am far from astroparticle physics and will not pretend to judge the diffuse-flux case in detail. I do see that you have stated your own difficulty frankly, that Baikal and AMANDA complicate credit and that most of the flux has no identified source. I would encourage you to say whether you could accept B012 as the committee's choice, since your statement that you would not block it carries weight. For my part I am now willing to move to that same position.

uncertainties: Priority for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks (Katori, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Ye) cannot be settled from my own knowledge, and I would like the record checked before the final ballot.
Whether the two-name credit should be accompanied by wording that divides the accuracy and many-body results (Ye) from the proposal and early demonstrations (Katori).

Whether the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes make a lattice-clock award look repetitive to those outside the metrology community; I think a narrow citation answers this, but I may be too close to the argument of the majority.
Whether B036 will be settled enough for a later year once the pairing mechanism and experimental credit are clearer.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I work in electronic-structure theory and magnetism at Uppsala and have no stated personal or institutional link to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer or the other shortlisted candidates. I am closer in field to the condensed-matter candidates (B036, B005, B057), and I changed my preference away from one of them, B036, on the scientific record. I note the lineage and affiliation disclosures made by Kroll and Olsson on B012 and see no need for a procedural step beyond recording them.
